S05 Sprint Report

This report covers QC, phasing, KIR and TRB germline genetics in the All of Us long-read cohort. The sprint ran from 6 to 12 October 2026 (scripts 50–65) and answered the supervisor's asks from the 6 October meeting:

  • exact counts;
  • whether the phased haplotypes can be trusted;
  • KIR by ancestry;
  • regional coverage;
  • the TRBV4-3 question.

Every method is explained in the background course, and every result carries its data trail. An independent review checked the work, and its corrections are built in.

The answers, with how sure each one is

Class II and B~C haplotypes on one contig are reliable; anything with HLA-A is not

In 179 trios, fewer than 20 of 248–262 one-contig DQ, DR–DQ, DP and B~C gene pairs mixed DNA from both parents. That puts the rate below ~7.7%; the true value is probably far lower, since the first 50 trios showed 0 of 69–76. Pairs that include HLA-A mixed parents ~40% of the time (Figure 5).How sure: high for the ranking. The 7.7% is a ceiling forced by masking, not a measured rate, and k-mer parent assignment has its own unmeasured error.

2-field typing disagrees in ~4% of relative checks, so roughly 2% of calls are wrong

Relative pairs and parent–child checks both fail in ~4% of genes (4.09% vs 4.15%). Each check compares two calls, so the per-call error is about half of that. Full resolution (4 fields) fails ~3× more often. A confidence score ≥ 4 cuts the error by 37–50% and keeps 91% of relative pair-genes (Figure 8).How sure: moderate. It is a lower bound, because errors that keep alleles shared are invisible. The two estimates share people, so they are not fully independent.

The "many novel HLA proteins" headline does not survive

4,250 classical protein-novel sequences shrink to 0 that are recurrent, clean and common. Of the recurrent ones, 4 have read support at non-homopolymer sites, and 2 of those (both DPB1) have since been named in IPD-IMGT/HLA. That leaves 2 still-unnamed candidates with clean read support, or 7 if homopolymer-class support is accepted. In 345 calls, the caller's two coding-sequence outputs disagree by a frame-changing indel, source undetermined (Figure 17).How sure: high that the headline fails. The read evidence comes from the same HiFi reads that built the assembly, so it is support, not independent proof. The 2 DPB1 alleles named later are a good sign that the pipeline finds real alleles.

No cross-group DQ haplotype exists on intact chromosomes

Cross-group DQA1~DQB1 pairs appear almost only across contig breaks, and the few on one contig are structurally abnormal. The haplotype atlas finds the DQ and DR51/52/53 rules without being told them (Figure 20).How sure: high for "no evidence of cross-group haplotypes". This shows absence, not the folding biology behind it.

Coverage is not a usable filter, but it is not irrelevant

The MHC and KIR run 12–17% below genome depth in nearly everyone. Lower depth goes with more fragmented KIR (34% → 55%), partly because haplotypes with fewer genes give lower depth. No cutoff removes a useful share of bad calls, so no filter is applied (Figure 11).Corrected after review: the first draft said depth "explains none". That conclusion was guaranteed by the rule's arithmetic.

TRBV4-3 absence is common and ancestry-structured, but the repertoire numbers don't add up yet

No germline copy: EUR 19.5%, AMR 30.1%, MID ~32%, EAS 37.1%, AFR 38.5%, SAS 55.1%. The ranking matches who never uses the gene, in the same order in all six groups. But fewer people never use it (27%) than lack it (33%), which cannot happen if both measures were exact. The repertoire count is a known lower bound, and some 0-copy calls may be wrong (Figure 30).How sure: high for the ranking, moderate for the exact AFR and SAS rates. "Consistent with the deletion driving non-use" is as far as the data go; proving it needs the per-person test (script 60), which waits on Aleix.

Decisions only Marc can make

Each item is a proposal with a recommendation; items 1–4 are also open entries in context/DECISIONS.md. The sprint's code supports every option. The consequence of saying no is given too.

  1. Ancestry-purity rule. Recommended: run the primary analyses on predicted ancestry, with p ≥ 0.95 as a sensitivity analysis. If you require p ≥ 0.95 everywhere instead: EUR and MID drop to 38% of their people, while SAS keeps 93% (Figure 1).
  2. Demote classical protein-novel counts to a resource table, and name only the read-supported candidates (2 unnamed plus 2 since named in IPD-IMGT/HLA). Recommended: yes. If no: a reviewer can show that most of the counts are homopolymer artefacts.
  3. KIR haplotype claims only on complete haplotypes (75%), with gene presence also reported from any contig as a check. Recommended: yes. If no: broken contigs pass for absent genes.
  4. Physical-haplotype rule. DQ, DR–DQ, DP and B~C may be used from one contig. A~B and A~C need statistical phasing or trios. DQ–DP is flagged. Recommended: yes. Cole's units (62) already follow it.
  5. No coverage filter. Accept that depth is a structure marker, not a usable QC cut. Recommended: yes.
  6. TRB genotyper. Switch from fixed cuts to the new mixture model, which allows for the read-capture bias, once 65b checks it against assemblies. Recommended: yes.
  7. Long jobs (Sequel II re-call, full ASE, genome-wide trio phasing). They are planned and costed in Long jobs, for you to discuss. None was run.
  8. Small allele counts. Counts of distinct allele sequences below 20 (for example "4 candidates") count alleles, not people, so they are shown exactly. Decide whether to mask them in published figures.

Before readingHow to read this report

The report has three layers. Read the summary first. Then use the background course as a reference: open a module whenever a result relies on an idea you have not met. Every result section uses the same three blocks.

Data trail (blue edge)

This block traces each result from start to finish:

  • which file it started from, and what one row of that file is;
  • what was done to it, step by step;
  • which trade-offs were made and why;
  • which unit was counted (people, haplotypes, calls, allele sequences) and over which denominator.

That last point is the "axis" a big dataset gets collapsed onto. If you know it, you know what a percentage means.

Figure caption

Shows describes what is drawn. How to read says where to look. Meaning gives the interpretation and the numbers. Limits says what the figure cannot tell you.

Significance (dashed box)

How big the effect is and how sure we are, measured against something you can picture. It also says what changes for the paper because of it.

Review (red edge)

An independent review checked the methods, the numbers and the wording. Where it found a problem, the red block says what was wrong and what changed.

Every number comes from a committed table in the public repo; the file is named under each figure. Counts of 1–19 people are never shown (see masking). Allele names and sequence counts are not people and are shown as is.

Background courseTen short modules

Each module explains one idea the results depend on, with a small picture. They are folded so the page stays compact. "Open all" in the contents column unfolds everything.

The data each person has, and how an HLA call is made

About 13,000 All of Us participants were sequenced with PacBio HiFi long reads. These are reads of ~15–20 kb that are about 99.9% accurate. For each person All of Us provides several files, and the project's earlier pipeline built one table on top of them.

What a row of Table 1 says. On haplotype 1 of person X, on contig h1tg000012l at positions S–E, there is HLA-DQB1 copy 1, and its sequence best matches DQB1*06:02:01:01. When nothing in the database matches exactly, the row records how it differs (novelty_depth, explained in MHC and HLA alleles). It records the exact coding change (cds_mut), how far the sequence is from the closest known allele (template_distance), whether the caller was unsure (template_warning), and whether several known alleles tied (n_tied).

Where the work runs. Participant-level files never leave the All of Us Workbench, a cloud VM. Scripts run there and write two kinds of output. INTERNAL tables (one row per person) stay on the VM. PUBLIC tables are aggregates, with small counts masked; these are copied into this public repo, and every figure is drawn from them.

Three sequencing platforms. Revio (newest, 11,015 people with calls) and Sequel IIe (1,218) went through the production pipeline. The 991 Sequel II people have assemblies but no HLA or KIR calls; Part 10 explains why. The platform also stands for the sequencing site, the period and the assembler version, so a "platform effect" mixes all of these.

Assembly, haplotypes, contigs and phasing

You carry two copies of chromosome 6, one from each parent. A haplotype is the sequence of one of those copies. The question "which alleles sit together on the same copy?" is called phasing. It matters because HLA genes act, and are inherited, as combinations along one chromosome.

The assembler (hifiasm) overlaps reads into long continuous pieces called contigs. Where the two parental copies differ, it separates them, so it produces two sets of contigs, labelled hap1 and hap2. Where the copies are identical over a long stretch, the reads cannot tell the copies apart and the contig usually ends. The next contig is then labelled hap1 or hap2 arbitrarily: hap1 of the next piece may be the other parent's copy.

So two kinds of "same haplotype" exist. If two genes sit on one contig, they are physically phased: one stretch of DNA joins them. If they sit on different contigs that merely share the label "hap1", nothing ties them together. In the picture, hap1 pairs A and B correctly but joins them to the mother's C. That is why the report keeps asking "same contig?", and why Part 2 measures how often one contig really holds one parent's DNA.

Two error types are measured later. A switch error is a short flip from one parent's sequence to the other inside a contig. A hamming error is the share of a contig that belongs to the "wrong" parent overall, which captures long-range mixing.

The MHC, HLA genes, allele names and "novel" alleles

The MHC is a ~4 Mb region of chromosome 6 that holds the HLA genes. Their proteins show fragments of proteins (peptides) to T cells. Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) is on nearly all cells and presents to CD8 T cells. Class II (DR, DQ, DP) is on immune cells and presents to CD4 T cells. They are the most variable genes in the human genome, and the strongest genetic risk factors for most autoimmune diseases.

Reading an allele name

"Novel" alleles and novelty depth. When the sequence matches no named allele, Immuannot reports the closest one and the level at which they differ. Novelty depth 2 means a new protein (the amino acids differ). Depth 3 means the same protein with a silent DNA change. Depth 4 means a difference outside the coding sequence only. A key is one distinct novel sequence: gene plus exact coding change. Five people carrying the same new sequence are one key with five carriers. Keys count alleles, not people.

DQ pairing groups (G1/G2). The DQ molecule is built from two chains, α (from DQA1) and β (from DQB1). Biochemistry says only some α/β combinations fold into a working molecule. Group 1 (G1) is DQA1*02–06 with DQB1*02–04. Group 2 (G2) is DQA1*01 with DQB1*05–06. Cross-group pairs are thought not to work, and a haplotype that encodes one is expected to be rare or absent. Part 6 tests that.

DR paralogs. Next to DRB1, a chromosome carries none or one of DRB3, DRB4 or DRB5, depending on the DRB1 lineage. These are the DR51 (DRB5), DR52 (DRB3) and DR53 (DRB4) haplotype groups. It is a known rule, so a method that finds it on its own is working (Part 6).

KIR genes and KIR haplotypes

KIR genes (on chr19) encode receptors on natural killer cells that read HLA class I molecules. Unlike HLA, KIR haplotypes differ in which genes they carry at all, not only in alleles: a chromosome carries roughly 7 to 15 KIR genes. Four framework genes are present on nearly every haplotype and mark its structure: KIR3DL3 at the start (centromeric end), 3DP1 and 2DL4 in the middle, and 3DL2 at the end (telomeric end).

Why KIR is hard to assemble. KIR genes are near-copies of each other (~90–98% identical), so contigs often stop inside the cluster. A complete haplotype in this report has all its KIR genes on one contig, with both end genes (3DL3 and 3DL2) present. Only on complete haplotypes can we say a gene is truly absent; elsewhere, "missing" may mean the contig ended early.

Allelic pairs. 2DL2 and 2DL3 are two forms of the same position, as are 3DL1 and 3DS1. A haplotype normally carries one or the other. Seeing both on one haplotype is either a rare real duplication or an assembly artefact, and Part 8 tells them apart.

The TRB locus, V(D)J recombination and the T-cell repertoire

Each T cell carries a T-cell receptor built from a β chain and an α chain. The β chain gene TRB (chr7, ~0.6 Mb) is stored in pieces: about 65 V segments (TRBV…), 2 D, 13 J and 2 C. As each T cell matures, it cuts its own DNA and joins one V to one D and one J. This is V(D)J recombination, and it permanently deletes the DNA between the joined pieces in that cell. A person's repertoire is the mix of receptors across their T cells, and RNA sequencing can measure how often each V segment is used.

Two facts follow, and both appear in the results. First, a gene that is missing from the germline cannot be used. About 27% of people never use TRBV4-3 (Aleix's repertoire work), and TRBV4-3 sits on a known optional insertion; Part 9 measures who carries it. Second, blood DNA is partly T-cell DNA. Because recombination deletes the segments between the joined V and J, the read depth over the D–J region and the nearby V genes is somatically reduced. That is not a germline genotype (Part 4).

Reference genome detail. The standard reference, GRCh38, describes the chromosome without the insertion. The insertion exists only on an "alternative" contig (ALT, named KI270803v1). The HiFi reads were aligned to GRCh38 without ALTs, so reads from TRBV4-3 have no matching place in the reference, and that complicates genotyping.

Reads, depth, mapping quality, alignment identity and allele fraction

Aligning reads to the reference stacks them over the positions they came from. The number of reads covering a base is the depth. Here it is about 20 on average.

  • Relative depth divides a region's depth by the same person's depth over neutral control windows. That cancels how much DNA that person was sequenced with. 1.0 means "covered like the rest of the genome". A one-copy deletion should give 0.5 and a duplication 1.5.
  • Mapping quality (MAPQ) is the aligner's confidence that a read is placed correctly. It is 0 when a read fits equally well in two places (paralogs) and up to 60 when the placement is unique. Counting depth at MAPQ ≥ 0 keeps ambiguous reads; MAPQ ≥ 20 drops them.
  • Alignment identity is the share of matching bases in an alignment block. Contig-to-reference alignments come in a table format called PAF, one line per block, which lists the matching bases and the block length. True copies of a region align at ~95–99.9%. Repeats that merely resemble it align much lower (Part 10).
  • Allele fraction: at a site where two versions exist, it is the share of reads that carry one version. A heterozygote should show ~0.5 and a homozygote 0 or 1. Each read is a draw, so with 14 reads a true 0.5 still scatters roughly between 0.3 and 0.7.

Homopolymers: the main HiFi error

A homopolymer is a run of one repeated base, like AAAAAAA. HiFi reads and assemblers sometimes miscount its length by one. A 1-base insertion or deletion inside a gene's coding sequence shifts the reading frame and produces a "new protein" that does not exist. Part 5 shows this artefact explains most recurrent "novel" classical HLA proteins.

Relatives, kinship, the unrelated set, trios and k-mers

Kinship coefficient. This is the probability that an allele picked at random from person 1 and one from person 2 at the same position are copies of the same ancestral allele. It is 0.5 for identical twins or duplicate samples, 0.25 for parent–child and full siblings, 0.125 for second degree and 0.0625 for third degree. All of Us provides it for every pair above ~0.044.

Unrelated set. Frequencies must not count one family several times. Pairs with kinship ≥ 0.0442 (the usual third-degree cut, 2−4.5) are broken by repeatedly removing the person with the most relatives. Among HLA-called people this leaves 11,856.

Trios. When a sequenced person has two first-degree relatives who are not related to each other, those two must be the parents. This finds 179 parent–parent–child trios.

k-mers and parent of origin (yak). A k-mer is a short word of DNA, here 31 letters. The tool yak lists all k-mers in each parent's reads. A k-mer in the child's contig that occurs only in the father's reads marks that stretch as paternal; one only in the mother's marks it maternal. Colouring a child's contig this way shows directly whether it is one parent's DNA, and so whether phasing is right.

Mendelian check. A child's allele must be present in the parent who transmitted it. If the transmitting parent (known from the k-mers) does not carry the child's called allele, then the child's call or the parent's call is wrong.

Population genetics: frequencies, Hardy–Weinberg, LD and ancestry labels

Allele frequency is the share of chromosomes (haplotypes) carrying an allele. With two chromosomes per person, 11,856 unrelated people give 23,712 haplotypes.

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium (HWE). If an insertion has frequency p and people pair their chromosomes at random, the expected genotype shares are p² (two copies), 2p(1−p) (one copy) and (1−p)² (none). Real populations follow this closely for most variants. A big shortage of heterozygotes usually means the genotyping is wrong, or that a group mixes sub-populations with different frequencies (the Wahlund effect).

Linkage disequilibrium (LD). Alleles of nearby genes are inherited together across generations, so some combinations are far more common, and others far rarer, than chance predicts. In the MHC, LD spans megabases. The expected count under independence is E = n × pA × pB: how often a combination would appear if the two genes were shuffled. Comparing it with the observed count shows LD. An observed 0 where E is 1,500 is a striking absence.

Predicted ancestry. All of Us assigns each person to one of six continental groups (AFR, AMR, EAS, EUR, MID, SAS) from genome-wide genetic similarity to reference panels. Each person also gets a probability for each group. "Purity p" is the highest of these. Admixed people, common in AMR, MID and EUR as labelled here, have lower p. These are genetic-similarity labels, not self-identity.

Statistics toolbox: every test used, in plain words
ToolWhat it answersHow to read it here
Proportion with a Wilson 95% CI"What share has X, and how precisely do we know it?"The interval is where the true share plausibly lies. Wilson behaves well even when the share is near 0% or 100%, or n is small. Example: 36 of 88 = 40.9% (31.2–51.4).
Upper bound from a masked count"At most how big can a masked rate be?"If fewer than 20 of 261 fail, the rate is below 19/261 = 7.3%. The report quotes the < 7.7% bound from 19/248, the smallest n among those pairs.
Odds ratio (OR)"How much more likely is X in group 1 than in group 2?"OR = 1 means no difference. OR 0.5 means the odds are halved. Odds are p/(1−p); for small p they are close to the probability itself.
Mantel–Haenszel ORAn OR computed within each stratum (here, each ancestry) and then combinedIt removes the part of a difference that only reflects different ancestry mixes between groups.
Spearman ρ"Does Y go up when X goes up?"It ranges from −1 to 1 and uses ranks, so outliers matter little. 0.72 is strong; 0.1–0.3 is weak.
Binomial test"Could this split of reads (or people) arise by chance from a fair 50:50?"A small p-value means chance alone is unlikely.
Bonferroni correctionMany tests at once give false hits by chanceDivide 0.05 by the number of tests. Part 6 calls a cell absent only if seeing 0 by chance is less likely than 0.05/m.
Resampling at equal N"Does group A have more alleles than B at the same sample size?"Larger samples always find more alleles, so each group is subsampled to the same N 50 times and the mean is compared.
Logistic regression OR per unit"Does lower depth raise the odds of a bad call?"Used in 59. An OR near 1 means depth does not predict the outcome.
HWE χ² test"Do genotype counts match p², 2pq, q²?"With thousands of people, tiny departures are "significant", so the size of the shortfall matters more than the p-value.
Small-count masking and complementary suppression

All of Us forbids publishing any count of 1–19 participants, because small groups can identify people. Such counts are written <20, and rates computed from them are blanked. Masking one cell is not enough when a table also shows its total and the other parts: the masked cell is a subtraction away. Complementary suppression then masks a second cell, written <20*, so the subtraction no longer works.

This sprint made the rule generic (_disclosure.py), applied it to every new public table and tested it. A few older tables still have the old problem; they are listed in Part 11.

Part 1The cohort, counted exactly

Question. How many people are in each analysis, by ancestry and platform, under each exclusion rule the repo uses? Until now every script picked its own rules, so the numbers did not line up. Script 50a builds one waterfall of exclusions, so a single list can be agreed.

From which file, by what process, counted how
Data in
cohort_membership.tsv (one row per long-read participant: platform, predicted ancestry, the six ancestry probabilities). Table 1 (hla_calls_rich.tsv) to see who has HLA calls. The relatedness pair list (kinship per related pair).
Process
  1. Start from all 13,252 cohort rows.
  2. Keep people with HLA calls.
  3. Build the unrelated set: break pairs with kinship ≥ 0.0442 by removing the most-connected person (background).
  4. Apply three purity thresholds, p ≥ 0.90, 0.95 and 0.98, where p is the probability of the assigned ancestry.
  5. Count each step overall, by ancestry and by platform.
Trade-offs
The purity thresholds were not chosen here: they are the three already used in older scripts, shown side by side so one can be picked. Greedy removal keeps more people than an optimal solution would lose, and it is deterministic.
Unit
People. Each bar shows people remaining after that step.

Two denominators you will meet. HLA analyses use 11,856 unrelated people, built from the 12,233 HLA-called people. KIR analyses (61) use 11,882 unrelated people, built from the 12,261 KIR-called people. The KIR set is slightly larger because a few people have KIR calls without HLA calls, and greedy removal depends on who is in the starting set. A single fixed unrelated list for every analysis is a cleanup item for the next sprint.

The All of Us relatedness file has disappeared from the v9 bucket. Unrelated sets now come from a cached copy of the same pairs, which script 11 saved. Scripts 59 and 61–65 use it through _s05_common.

SignificanceThe 991 missing Sequel II people are 24% of all AFR participants in the long-read cohort. Every AFR frequency in this report rests on 3,020 instead of ~4,000 unrelated people. Their 95% intervals are about 15% wider than they would be with everyone, and if Sequel II AFR people differ from Revio AFR people (another site, another period), estimates may be biased too.

Part 2Can we trust the phased haplotypes?

Question. Every haplotype claim in the project assumes that genes sitting on one contig came from one parent: the DQ rule, the atlas, Cole's fine-mapping units, the KIR haplotypes. Is that true, and for which gene pairs? Three checks answer it, each stricter than the last:

  1. how often two genes share a contig at all (50b);
  2. whether a one-contig haplotype in one relative appears intact in the other (56b);
  3. the direct truth from trios: which parent each gene came from (57, 57b).
Check 1: how often two genes share a contig (50b)
Data in
Table 1, copy-1 calls of 25 MHC genes, all 12,233 people (relatives included, which is fine for a structural question).
Process
For each haplotype and each gene pair with both genes called, ask "same contig name?". Average over haplotypes, overall and per platform. Also count how many different contigs carry MHC genes on each haplotype.
Trade-offs
This measures co-location, not correctness: a wrongly joined contig counts as "same contig". Checks 2 and 3 measure correctness.
Unit
Haplotypes, ~24,000 per gene pair. The percentage is haplotypes with both genes on one contig / haplotypes with both genes called.
Output
50_qc_foundation/same_contig_matrix.tsv, mhc_contigs_per_hap.tsv
Check 2: relatives (56b)
Data in
Table 1 plus the relatedness pairs. 569 first-degree pairs (kinship 0.177–0.354), both people HLA-called.
Process
  1. Keep pairs that share an MHC haplotype: at most 1 of 8 classical genes without a shared allele. Siblings who inherited different haplotypes share nothing and would look like errors.
  2. For each gene pair (DQA1~DQB1, DRB1~DQB1, DPA1~DPB1, B~C, A~B), take haplotypes where both relatives have the two genes on one contig.
  3. Ask whether the one-contig combination seen in relative 1 is found intact in relative 2.
Trade-offs
All of Us gives no IBD0 information, so parents and siblings cannot be told apart. Keeping only haplotype-sharing pairs removes the IBD0 siblings, but it also drops pairs where two genes are mistyped. That pushes the measured error down a little; the first draft wrongly said it did not bias.
Unit
Haplotype tests (one gene pair in one relative pair). n = 68 (A~B) to 435 (DPA1~DPB1).
Output
56_phasing_typing_benchmark/refined_sweep.tsv
Check 3: trios, the direct truth (57, 57b)
Data in
For 179 trios: the child's hap1/hap2 contigs (assembly FASTA), the child's Table 1 rows, and both parents' HiFi reads (BAM).
Process
  1. Build k-mer databases (31-letter words, yak count) from each parent's reads over a padded window: the MHC, KIR and all of chr20 as a genome-wide control.
  2. 57, region level: run yak trioeval on the child's contig pieces to get switch and hamming error (background). This was done for 50 trios.
  3. 57b, gene level: for every child HLA gene, count paternal-only and maternal-only k-mers within ±10 kb. Assign the parent with ≥ 5 k-mers and ≥ 3× the other, otherwise "ambiguous".
  4. For each one-contig gene pair, ask whether the two genes came from different parents.
Trade-offs
k-mer databases cover only the windows, so k-mers from paralogs elsewhere are missed (this inflates error slightly). 10–31% of genes get no parent (ambiguous) and drop out. The k-mer assignment itself can be wrong, and no test here measures how often; that is a gap the review flagged.
Unit
Gene pairs on one contig in a child: n = 81–262 per pair.
Output
57_yak_trioeval/trioeval_summary.tsv, pair_phase_truth.tsv, gene_origin_summary.tsv

Significance

This is the result the rest of the project stands on. Class II is the best-phased region in the genome sample. Any DQ or DR–DQ statement can therefore use one-contig haplotypes, and so can Cole's fine-mapping units.

Any class I haplotype claim that involves HLA-A, including the older A~B~C extended-haplotype and A–B LD tables, is wrong in about 4 of 10 haplotypes. Those results need statistical phasing before they are used.

The zero cross-group DQ count in Part 6 is itself evidence for good phasing. If phasing mixed parents at random even 5% of the time, artefactual cross-group pairs would appear by the hundreds.

What the review changed here
  • "Fewer than 7.7%" is now described as a masking ceiling, not an estimate.
  • The wrong claim that the relative filter introduces no bias was removed: the filter lowers the measured error a little.
  • The uncalibrated error of k-mer parent assignment is now stated as a limit.
  • The switch-error comparison across regions is now qualified.

Part 3Can we trust the allele calls?

Question. When the caller says a person carries HLA-DQB1*06:02, how often is that wrong? There is no truth set for 12,000 people, so error is measured from inheritance, which does not depend on the caller.

  • Two relatives who share a haplotype must carry the same allele at every gene on it.
  • A child's allele must be present in the parent who passed it on.

Either way, a failure means at least one of the two calls is wrong.

The confidence score (56): what each point means
Data in
Table 1 (hla_calls_rich.tsv: one row per person × haplotype × gene, with the contig name, the distance to the closest known allele, warning flags and the platform).
Process
Each call gets one point for each of seven properties that a priori make a call more trustworthy:
  1. it shares a contig with its phasing partner gene;
  2. its haplotype's MHC sits on ≤ 2 contigs;
  3. its distance to the nearest known allele is ≤ the cohort's 75th percentile;
  4. its difference from that allele is not only a homopolymer indel;
  5. the caller raised no template warning;
  6. there was no tie between candidate alleles;
  7. it came from Revio.
The score is 0–7, and a claim can then use only calls at or above a threshold.
Trade-offs
The seven points are equally weighted, chosen before seeing error rates, not fitted. A fitted score (for example a logistic model on trio errors) would separate better but would need held-out trios to be honest.
Unit
A call (one gene on one haplotype in one person).
Output
A score column used by 56b and 57b. The per-call scores stay on the VM.
Relatives check (56b) and trio check (57b): data and processing
Data in
56b: the 569 first-degree pairs from Part 2, both HLA-called. 57b: the 179 trios, with each child gene's parent of origin from k-mers (Part 2, check 3).
Process
56b: per gene, ask "do the two relatives share at least one 2-field allele?". Pairs failing at ≥ 2 classical genes are dropped as probable non-sharers (siblings with no haplotype in common), and the rate of genes with no shared allele is reported. 57b: per child gene with a known parent of origin, ask "is the child's allele among that parent's two alleles?", at 2 fields and at full resolution.
Trade-offs
56b: dropping pairs with ≥ 2 failing genes removes true non-sharers, but also pairs with two real typing errors. That pushes the measured error down. With ~4% error per gene over 8 genes, roughly a quarter of errors sit in such pairs, so the true pair rate could be ~5%, not 4.09%. 57b: only HiFi parents are used, and genes without an assigned parent (10–31%) drop out.
Unit
A pair-gene (56b, n = 6,455 at score 0) or a child gene (57b, n = 3,611). Each compares two calls, so the error per single call is about half of what is shown.
Output
56_phasing_typing_benchmark/refined_sweep.tsv, pair_sharing_distribution.tsv; 57_yak_trioeval/mendel_typing.tsv
Significance

The measurement is collapsed onto one axis: the % of comparisons where two calls that should agree do not. About 4% of pair comparisons fail at 2 fields, so a single call is wrong roughly 2–2.5% of the time, and more for MICA and DRB3. That is low enough for population frequencies (an error spreads thinly over many alleles) but not negligible for rare-allele claims. A rare allele seen in 10 people could be partly made of errors from a common neighbour.

Full resolution is about 3× worse. Any claim at the third or fourth field (synonymous or intronic novelty, expression by exact allele) should carry read support or use the score.

What the review changed here
  • "Two independent methods agree" became "two related checks on overlapping people agree".
  • The per-call error is now stated as about half the pair rate.
  • The relative filter is now described as biasing the error down, with an estimate of how much.
  • "Halves the error" became "cuts it by 37–50%", because trios fall less than relatives.

Part 4Coverage over the immune regions

Question. The supervisor asked for a regional coverage filter: flag people whose MHC (or KIR) depth is far below their genome depth, on the theory that thin regions give bad calls. Script 58 measured depth for everyone. Script 59 then asked whether thin coverage explains the calls we distrust, and whether a cutoff would remove a useful share of them.

From which file, by what process (58)
Data in
Each person's HiFi BAM aligned to GRCh38 without ALT contigs, read in place from the bucket (12,233 people). A BED file of 137 regions: the MHC window chr6:29.5–33.5 Mb, the KIR window on chr19, every HLA, KIR and TRB gene (GENCODE v46), and 5 control windows elsewhere in the genome.
Process
  1. samtools bedcov sums read bases per region, at MAPQ ≥ 0 (all reads) and ≥ 20 (confidently placed reads).
  2. Mean depth = bases ÷ region length.
  3. Relative depth = region depth ÷ the median of the person's 5 control windows. So 1.0 means "as covered as the rest of this person's genome".
  4. Summaries by ancestry and platform; TRB per-gene histograms and copy-number calls (cuts 0.25 and 0.75).
Trade-offs
Dividing by the person's own control depth removes differences in sequencing amount between people, so thin means "thin for this person". MAPQ 0 counts reads that could map in several places; MAPQ 20 drops them. Both are shown. KIR genes that GRCh38 carries only on ALT contigs cannot be measured on these BAMs.
Unit
A person × region value. Every figure collapses it to the distribution across people.
Output
58_regional_depth/depth_summary_by_region.tsv, trb_rel_depth_histogram.tsv, trb_cn_by_ancestry.tsv. Per-person depths stay on the VM.

Is thin coverage behind the bad calls? Partly, but no filter helps

From which file, by what process (59)
Data in
58's per-person depths (VM), joined to per-person outcome flags derived from Table 1 and the KIR annotation, for the 11,856 unrelated people.
Process
  1. Normalise each window's relative depth to the cohort median for the same region and platform, so 1.0 = typical for that region.
  2. Flag eight outcomes per person: KIR haplotype incomplete; KIR framework gene missing; an HLA gene absent; an empty haplotype; DQ genes split across contigs; anomalous DQ spacing; a cross-group DQ pair; MHC on ≥ 7 contigs. A negative control is added: framework gene missing on a complete KIR haplotype, which should be biology, not assembly.
  3. Outcome rate per 0.1 depth bin, with Wilson CIs.
  4. Logistic regression per outcome: odds ratio per 0.1 lower depth, adjusted for platform and ancestry.
  5. A cutoff scan under a rule fixed in advance: remove ≥ 50% of an outcome's events while removing ≤ 10% of people, overall and in every ancestry with ≥ 100 people.
Trade-offs
The rule was meant to accept a filter only if it was clearly worth it. The review showed it could never pass for a common outcome: removing 10% of people can remove at most 10/p% of events, where p is the outcome's prevalence. For KIR incomplete (p ≈ 38%) that ceiling is 26%. The "no filter" conclusion therefore came from arithmetic, not from the data. The logistic odds ratios and the rate-by-bin curves are the real test.
Unit
A person. Rates are % of people in a depth bin with the outcome.
Output
59_depth_outcome_join/vm_2026-10-12/: outcome_by_depth_bin.tsv, logistic_or.tsv, cutoff_scan.tsv, proposed_cutoff.tsv
Significance

Coverage is a structure marker, not a QC knob. The useful consequences:

  • No coverage filter is applied, and 61 and 62 were run with an exclusion list of 0 people.
  • Depth can be used as a covariate in KIR models.
  • A methods paragraph can say exactly this: low depth goes with KIR fragmentation, partly because contracted haplotypes lower depth, and no cutoff removes a useful share of problem calls without removing real biology.

The TRB locus: what depth can and cannot say

What the review changed here
  • The first draft said depth "explains none" of the bad calls and that thin people have them "at roughly the cohort-wide rate". Both were wrong: the decision rule could not pass for common outcomes, and the logistic models show clear associations. The section was rewritten around the rate curves and odds ratios, with the reverse-causation reading.
  • "7–8% better" became "about 7 points (~9%)".
  • "About half the cohort" became "59%".

Part 5Novel HLA alleles: what survives

Question. The earlier figures counted thousands of "novel" HLA alleles, meaning sequences not in the allele database. Before any of them becomes a headline, three questions need answers:

  1. Do they recur in unrelated people? A one-off is more likely an error.
  2. Do they avoid the known HiFi error class, a 1-base insertion or deletion in a run of one repeated base (a homopolymer, background)?
  3. Do the person's own reads carry them?

Script 50d asked the first two. Script 64 re-matched every key against IPD-IMGT/HLA 3.65.0 (July 2026, 10 releases newer than the 3.55.0 the caller used) and tested up to 5 carriers per key against the HiFi reads.

From which file, by what process (50d and 64)
Data in
Table 1 rows flagged protein-novel (the protein differs from every known one) or synonymous-novel (same protein, new DNA). The cds_mut string records how the called coding sequence differs from Immuannot's nearest known allele. For 64 there are also the person's assembly (<hap>.trimmed.fa), Immuannot's GTF and its cds.fa.gz record, the IPD 3.65.0 FASTA and allele history, and the HiFi BAM.
Process
  1. Key = (gene, cds_mut): one distinct novel sequence. The funnel counts keys, not people.
  2. Filters in order: ≥ 2 unrelated carriers; not homopolymer-indel-only; no template warning; seen on ≥ 2 platforms; in ≥ 2 ancestries (64 only); ≥ 20 clean carriers.
  3. 64 re-match: rebuild the CDS from the GTF exon rows on the contig and compare it with the cds.fa.gz record. If they disagree, the call is skipped and counted (the "CDS disagree" class). Then look for an exact match in 3.65.0: "now known" means the allele was named after 3.55.0.
  4. 64 read test: build two versions of the person's local haplotype, the called one (Wc) and the same one with the novel differences reverted to the nearest known allele (Tn). Align each spanning HiFi read to both. A read "supports" if it fits Wc better and "contradicts" if it fits Tn better. A call is supported with ≥ 3 reads assigned to that haplotype and ≥ 70% support, and contradicted at ≤ 15%. A key's reads are also pooled across its tested carriers.
Trade-offs
At most 5 carriers per key keeps the run small (4,616 calls) but means a key's verdict rests on few people. The reads are the same HiFi reads the assembly was built from, so read support is consistency, not independent proof. Short reads (a different chemistry) would be the independent test; they were not run.
Unit
Keys (distinct sequences) in the funnels; calls (one gene in one person) in the outcome figure; reads in the homopolymer figure.
Output
50_qc_foundation/protein_novel_waterfall.tsv; 64_novel_allele_validation/tables/ (funnel_with_evidence.tsv, failures_summary.tsv, hp_runlength_by_gene.tsv)
Significance

The axis here is distinct sequences surviving each test. Starting from thousands of classical "new proteins", the evidence supports a handful: 2 unnamed with clean read support and 2 since confirmed by IPD. Everything else is either a homopolymer indel the reads cannot settle, a mismatch between the caller's two outputs, or undecided at this depth.

For the paper, protein-novel counts belong in a resource table, not a headline. The new QC finding is the 345 record-vs-exon disagreements. It applies to anyone using Immuannot's CDS output, and is worth a methods note once the source is pinned down.

What the review changed here
  • "4–9 real recurrent alleles" became "2 unnamed with clean read support, 2 since named, up to 7 with homopolymer-class support".
  • The homopolymer read figure is now marked as confounded. The code was fixed (hp_* now counts only reads assigned to the haplotype), and a rerun is planned.
  • "The frameshift is in the record, not the genome" became "source undetermined".
  • The 50d vs 64 funnel difference is now stated, not hidden.
  • Exact call counts in the outcome figure were rounded so a masked count cannot be recovered by subtraction.

Part 6MHC haplotype biology

The DQ G1/G2 pairing rule survives an ascertainment check

DQ molecules are built from one DQA1 and one DQB1 chain. Alleles fall into two groups (G1 and G2, background), and a G1 alpha chain does not pair well with a G2 beta chain. Script 37 found 0 cross-group DQA1~DQB1 haplotypes among 17,255 physically phased ones. A sceptic could argue that cross-group haplotypes exist but break contigs more often, so they are under-counted. Script 50e tested this.

From which file, by what process (50e)
Data in
Table 1 DQA1 and DQB1 calls, both haplotypes of every HLA-called person, with contig names and positions.
Process
For each haplotype label (hap1 or hap2), take the DQA1 and DQB1 calls, classify each allele as G1 or G2, and record whether the two genes sit on the same contig. If they do not, the pairing of a DQA1 with a DQB1 under one label is only as good as the assembler's labelling across a break: effectively random. The split rate is compared between within-group and cross-group pairs, and the observed cross-group share among split haplotypes is compared with the share expected if labels were random.
Trade-offs
Haplotypes, not people, so relatives add near-duplicates; that does not affect a structural question. The ≥ 100 kb spacing check was a VM inspection whose script is not committed.
Unit
Haplotypes (~22,000 with both genes called).
Output
50_qc_foundation/dq_ascertainment.tsv

An atlas of combinations that never occur

From which file, by what process (52)
Data in
Table 1, one-contig gene pairs only (both genes on the same contig of the same haplotype), at field 1 (allele lineage, e.g. DQA1*01).
Process
  1. For each gene pair, count each lineage × lineage combination.
  2. Expected count under independence: E = (rows total × column total) ÷ grand total.
  3. If a combination is truly allowed, seeing 0 has probability e−E. Call it "absent" if e−E passes a Bonferroni-corrected threshold and it is absent pooled and in ≥ 2 ancestries, each with ≥ 200 haplotypes.
Trade-offs
Independence is a null nobody believes for MHC genes, which have strong LD. So "absent" means "rarer than chance allows", not "impossible". Biology is a judgement on top.
Unit
Haplotypes.
Output
52_mhc_haplotype_atlas/absent_cells_field1.tsv, absent_pair_summary_field1.tsv

Why AMR shows more HLA alleles than AFR

Phased class II units for Cole's fine-mapping (62)

What the file contains, and how each row is made
Data in
Table 1 (DQA1, DQB1, DRB1 calls with contigs and positions), the unrelated list, 59's exclusion list (0 people), and the Part 2 trio rule.
Process
One row per person × haplotype × unit (DQA1~DQB1 and DRB1~DQA1~DQB1). Each row has the full and 2-field alleles and an evidence level: physical (all genes on one contig; trio-validated pair types), physical_flagged, split_contigs, or incomplete (a gene missing). It also has the DQ G1/G2 class, structural flags (anomalous_spacing ≥ 100 kb, anomalous_multicopy), a coverage flag (all pass) and an unrelated flag.
Trade-offs
The physical level inherits the uncalibrated k-mer origin error from Part 2. Relatives are kept (flagged), because fine-mapping models them, so the percentages below include related haplotypes.
Unit
Haplotype units (48,906 rows in total).
Output
The per-person table stays INTERNAL on the VM and nothing has been uploaded. Marc runs the upload to the in-perimeter bucket himself after checking the manifest. Data dictionary: reports/hla_popgen/62_cole_haplotype_units/README.md.
DQA1~DQB1 unitsAFREURAll
physical (one contig)91.4%92.4%92.8%
split across contigs3.0%2.0%2.1%
incomplete (a gene missing)5.7%5.7%5.1%

The other ancestries are 92.7–94.8% physical. Their split and incomplete shares are withheld, because together with the published G1/G2 counts they would reveal a count under 20.

The most common AFR unit is DQA1*01:02~DQB1*06:02 (18.4% of resolved AFR haplotypes). Tables: reports/hla_popgen/62_cole_haplotype_units/vm_2026-10-12/.

Significance

Cole can fine-map on physical DQ and DR–DQ haplotypes for about 93% of haplotypes, with a flag for the rest, instead of statistically phased guesses.

The absence of cross-group DQ haplotypes is the kind of hard zero that makes a strong figure. Next to an LD null model, it would show whether the constraint is stronger than LD alone predicts, which was idea #2 of the research-ideas note.

What the review changed here
  • The exact cross-group counts were removed: two numbers in the old text gave back a masked count. The underlying table is fixed too.
  • The Cole table no longer shows AMR, EAS and SAS split/incomplete values, which came from a superseded pull.
  • "No cross-group haplotype exists" became "none was found".
  • "Admixture explains" became "consistent with admixture".

Part 7Expression checks

Question. Blood RNA is a second, independent measurement. If the DNA says a person has two copies of a gene, the RNA should usually show more of it than in someone with one copy, and none in someone with zero. Two checks were run: presence/absence against expression (55), and a pilot of allele-specific expression on personal references (53).

From which file, by what process (55 and 53)
Data in
55: All of Us v9 RNA-SeQC gene TPM (whole blood, reads aligned to the standard reference), joined to DNA copy counts from Table 1 and the KIR annotation. 53: 80 unrelated people's RNA FASTQs, plus their own two HLA-A/B/C mRNA sequences from the assembly.
Process
55: count the haplotypes carrying the gene (0, 1, 2), then compare TPM across those groups (Spearman ρ). Only "strict" people are used, whose call is trustworthy: DRB5 in people whose DRB1–DQA1 sits on one contig on both haplotypes, and KIR in people with two complete haplotypes. 53: build a per-person reference from their two alleles of each gene, with every other MHC gene as a decoy. Align RNA reads (minimap2 short-read mode, MAPQ ≥ 10), count reads per allele, and test imbalance with a binomial test. Mapping bias is measured by aligning simulated reads from a perfectly balanced 1:1 mix.
Trade-offs
Standard TPM is computed on a reference that lacks many KIR paralogs, so it validates only genes whose paralogs are present. 53 used read 1 only and kept PCR duplicates, a pilot shortcut. Its exact sampling command was not recorded.
Unit
A person (55); a person × gene (53).
Output
55_structure_expression/structure_expression.tsv; 53_hla_ase_pilot/ase_by_gene_class.tsv
Significance

DRB5 shows that the DNA presence calls are right where the reference lets RNA check them.

The ASE pilot shows that personal references can measure allele imbalance in HLA with negligible mapping bias. That is the foundation for idea #3 (drivers of HLA allele-specific expression), but only after a cohort-scale run, which is a long job.

Part 8KIR: structure first, then the ancestry panel

Question. KIR haplotypes vary in gene content (background), so "gene absent" can mean real biology or a contig that stopped early. Script 51 checked which it is. Script 61 then made the ancestry panel on haplotypes that cannot be broken.

From which file, by what process (51 and 61)
Data in
Immuannot's KIR annotation (GTF) per haplotype: gene names, copies, contigs and positions, plus allele calls. 51 used all 24,513 haplotypes; 61 used the 11,882 unrelated KIR-called people (23,755 haplotypes).
Process
  1. Complete haplotype = all KIR calls on one contig, with both end genes 3DL3 and 3DL2 present. Such a haplotype cannot hide a gene in a gap.
  2. Class every haplotype: complete, multi-contig, or one contig with an open end.
  3. Framework-gene presence per class (51).
  4. Per ancestry, on complete haplotypes only (61): gene frequency, a "B-content" share, top alleles (protein field), and genes per haplotype.
Trade-offs
The complete-only rule removes fragmentation bias, but it can add another: if longer or more repetitive haplotypes (often B-content) break more often, complete haplotypes under-represent them. Completeness is close across ancestries (72–79%), so between-ancestry comparisons are fairly safe, but absolute B-content may be slightly low. For simple carrier frequencies, gene presence on any contig is robust to this and serves as a check.
Unit
Haplotypes. 11,882 unrelated is not the 11,856 of the HLA analyses: the greedy unrelated set is built from a different starting cohort (KIR-called vs HLA-called people).
Output
51_kir_structure_qc/; 61_kir_by_ancestry_panel/vm_2026-10-12/

KIR by ancestry, complete haplotypes only (61)

Of the 23,755 haplotypes, 17,905 (75.4%) are complete, from 72.3% (AFR) to 78.9% (EAS). The 59 list excluded nobody.

This is a KIR-by-ancestry panel from complete long-read haplotypes in ~12,000 people, with alleles. Most published KIR frequencies come from presence/absence typing of smaller, mostly European cohorts.

The strongest contrasts are EAS's A-richness and AFR's missing telomeric B block. Their KIR allele distributions differ more than their gene content does. Both are natural partners for the HLA results, since KIR receptors read HLA class I ligands.

What the review changed here
  • "cB share" is now called "B-content share": the gene set includes telomeric B genes.
  • The claim that each value is "0.4–1.6 points lower than 43" was misattributed. That range is the B-content share vs all haplotypes; gene frequencies run 2–9 points higher.

  • 11,882 vs 11,856 is explained.

Part 9The TRB germline insertion and TRBV4-3

Question. Aleix found that 27.3% of people never use TRBV4-3 in their T-cell repertoire, from SAS 43.5% down to EUR 16.7%. A known germline polymorphism, an optional ~21.7 kb insertion, carries TRBV4-3 together with TRBV3-2 and a second copy of TRBV6-2/6-3 (background). A person without the insertion on either chromosome cannot use TRBV4-3. How common is that, by ancestry? Does it account for the usage gap?

The deletion itself is in the literature. What would be new is ancestry-stratified long-read genotyping in ~11,000 diverse people, and, once script 60 runs, a per-person link to the same people's repertoires.

How each person was genotyped (65, reads mode), and the bias this created
Data in
Each person's HiFi reads over the TRB V cluster, read in place from the BAM (12,233 people), and the IMGT TRBV4-3 / TRBV3-2 probe sequences.
Process
  1. A reference read runs across the empty insertion site without a break: it covers the whole ~5.9 kb breakpoint interval plus ≥ 1 kb anchored on each side, ~7.9 kb in total. Only a chromosome without the insertion can produce one.
  2. An insertion read carries a TRBV4-3 (or TRBV3-2) probe hit at ≥ 97% identity. Only a chromosome with the insertion can produce one.
  3. Allele fraction (AF) = insertion reads ÷ (insertion + reference reads).
  4. Genotype by fixed cuts: 0 copies below 0.2, 1 copy from 0.2 to 0.8, 2 copies above 0.8. At least 6 informative reads are required (median 14).
Trade-offs
The two read types are not equally easy to get. A read of length L can contain the ~0.3 kb probe from about L + 0.3 kb of start positions, but can span the 7.9 kb reference requirement from only about L − 7.9 kb. For typical HiFi reads (L ≈ 18 kb) that is 18.3 vs 10.1, a 1.8:1 ratio, so a true heterozygote is expected at AF ≈ 1.8 ÷ 2.8 ≈ 0.64, not 0.5. The bias also changes with each person's read lengths, so no single fixed cut is right for everyone.
Unit
A person (genotype); allele frequency counts chromosomes.
Output
65_trb_assembly_genotype/reads_unrelated/ and reads_all/: genotype_by_stratum.tsv, allele_fraction_histogram.tsv

The fix: a genotyper that learns where heterozygotes sit

Instead of fixed cuts, the new --genotyper mixture fits three groups (0, 1, 2 copies) to each feature and platform at once. Each group has its own expected AF, so the het mode is learned (about 0.63 here) instead of assumed to be 0.5. It is a binomial mixture fitted by EM; a person is called only if their most likely group has ≥ 90% posterior probability, and otherwise is "ambiguous". It is written and tested (27 tests pass), and needs a VM run of a few minutes in aggregate mode.

A preview on the public histogram: the 0-copy rates barely move (AFR 38.5 → 38.3%, SAS 55.1 → 56.2%). The heterozygote deficit closes in EUR, AMR, EAS and MID (inbreeding-like coefficient F ≈ 0, EUR −0.02). It does not close in AFR (F ≈ 0.07) or SAS (F ≈ 0.10), which still have more 0-copy people than Hardy–Weinberg expects.

Two explanations for AFR and SAS are open. The insertion alleles there may be divergent enough to miss the 97%-identity probes, so heterozygotes would be called 0. Or there is real structure within those labels (several sub-populations with different frequencies pooled together, which always produces excess homozygotes). The 65b assembly comparison, stratified by ancestry, can tell these apart.

Why the bounds matter: 0-copy people have only the harder-to-capture reference reads, so they are more likely to fall under the 6-read floor and go uncalled. Significance

The axis is % of people with zero germline copies, set against % of people with zero repertoire use. The ranking agreement across six ancestries is strong evidence that the deletion matters. TRBV4-3 non-use in SAS, the highest of any group, is mostly explained by germline absence: 55% of SAS lack the gene entirely.

For any TCR study, TRBV4-3 usage differences between populations must be adjusted for germline copy number before being read as immunology. The per-person test (60) turns this from "consistent with" into a measured effect.

Script 60 is blocked needs Aleix

The per-person join is written and tested. It needs Aleix's W1 usage table, which is not on Marc's app: only per-person TRUST4 files are there. Aleix needs to copy the usage table (or vj_usage.pkl) to the bucket.

What the review changed here
  • The expected inequality was stated backwards ("never-use should be no higher than absence"). It is now correct, and the gap is reported and explained.
  • "The usage gap is a germline deletion" became "consistent with".
  • "Linked to their own repertoires" became "once 60 runs".
  • All six never-used rates are now shown, with their source.
  • The het deficit is now traced to a capture asymmetry built into the read rules, not "over-sampling". A genotyper that allows for it was written, and the AFR/SAS residual is reported.
  • No-call bounds were added.

Part 10The 991 Sequel II people (mostly AFR)

Question. Why do 991 people, about a quarter of AFR participants, have no HLA or KIR calls, and what would it take to call them?

Diagnosis and fix (63)
Data in
The long-read manifest and each person's assembly FASTA (SEQUEL2_DIAGNOSIS.md).
Process
Production extracts the MHC and KIR contigs from each assembly using the assembly-to-GRCh38 alignment. The Sequel II people have no such alignment, so they fell into a "self-align" tier that production skipped. That path was also broken in three ways:
  • their FASTAs are plain gzip, which samtools faidx cannot index;
  • a whole assembly aligned to chr6 alone pulled in 1.3–1.9 GB per haplotype instead of ~4 MB;
  • the reference was chr6-only, so KIR on chr19 could never match.
Script 63 fixes it in two stages. Stage 1 finds candidate contigs against a ±1 Mb slice of the reference. Stage 2 confirms them against the whole primary genome at MAPQ ≥ 20, with ≥ 10 kb blocks and a 25 MB size guard. Calls are then made with the same caller and settings as production.
Trade-offs
Self-alignment uses a different extraction route from production, so before pooling, ~20 Revio people should be run through it and compared with their production calls.
Status
The first 2-person smoke test stopped at the 25 MB guard, which did its job. Long repeat chains at low identity had passed stage 1 (in one haplotype, 17,011 of 17,053 blocks were below 0.8 identity, pulling in ~10,000 contigs). The real MHC contigs sit at 0.95–0.98 identity (42 contigs, 6.1 MB). Stage 1 now also requires block identity ≥ 0.8 (merged, with a test). The second smoke test runs as soon as the VM is back.
Significance

Every AFR frequency in this report rests on 3,020 unrelated people instead of ~4,000. If the Sequel II AFR people differ from the Revio AFR people (another site, another time), estimates may be biased too.

The re-call is the single job with the largest effect on the AFR results. It is also more than a day of compute, so it is planned, not run (see the next section).

Wrap-upIndependent review: what it found and what changed

Three reviewers checked this sprint's work, each with no stake in it.

  • A methods reviewer read the scripts against the claims (19 findings).
  • A numbers reviewer traced every number in the report to a committed table (41 findings).
  • A readability reviewer read it as you would.

Most numbers traced correctly. The serious findings were three conclusions stated more strongly than the data allow, one inverted piece of logic, and several ways small counts could be recovered by subtraction. Each is listed below with what was done.

Wrap-upLong jobs: plans and costs (nothing here was run)

This sprint ran no job longer than a day. Below is every job that would, or that is short but waits for the VM, with what it answers, how long it takes and what it costs. Costs use the current VM's rate ($0.37/h for 4 vCPU and 32 GB). Bigger machines are scaled from GCP list prices, so confirm them in the Workbench resize dialog. Each long job is resumable and can be cut into batches of a day or less, so none needs a multi-day unattended run.

1 · Re-call the 991 Sequel II people (63)

Answers: HLA and KIR for the missing quarter of AFR participants. It is the largest remaining bias in every AFR number. Measured so far: an estimated ~40 min per person per 4-vCPU worker, to be confirmed (with peak memory) by the second smoke test, which takes under an hour.

Part 11Disclosure and open items

Small-count masking: what this sprint did

Masking each count of 1–19 on its own is not enough (background). If a table shows a total and all its parts but one, the hidden part is a subtraction away. Earlier in the sprint, complementary suppression was added inside each table (_disclosure.py, used by 58, 59, 62 and 65): when exactly one cell of a sum is hidden, the next smallest is hidden too, shown as <20*.

The review found that this was still not enough, because sums also run across tables. Two examples:

  • 65's genotype counts equal sums of its allele-fraction bins;
  • 58's copy-number counts equal sums of its depth bins.

It also found such leaks in older tables (50 waterfall, DQ ascertainment, 51 allelic pairs, 53 ASE classes, 55 expression, 56 platform rows, 64 call outcomes). A cross-table masking step now re-masks the committed public tables, adding <20* where a hidden cell could be recovered. 65 and 58 now apply the cross-table sums themselves on future runs. The report text uses rounded percentages or omits values wherever a count could be recovered.

Known gaps after re-masking (checked with 66_cross_table_suppression.py --check):

  • MID's HLA-called and unrelated denominators (495 and 487) are both published in many tables, so the 8 related MID people can be worked out. Masking one table cannot hide that.
  • More generally, 65's reads_all minus reads_unrelated gives related-people counts cell by cell. Dropping reads_all from the public repo would fix it.
  • 64/tables/summary_by_stratum.tsv (counts of novel calls by gene, platform and ancestry) is not re-masked yet: too large for the solver as written.
  • Threshold sweeps (score t vs t+1, MAPQ 0 vs 20) and tables outside the review's list (56 threshold_sweep, 61, 62) are not modelled across tables yet.

Needs your decision flagged

The earlier, less-masked versions of these tables are still in the repo's git history, which is public. They can only be removed by rewriting history, and that has been ruled out so far. Options:

  1. accept the residual risk (aggregate counts, no identifiers);
  2. rewrite history on main (disruptive for Aleix's and Marc's clones);
  3. make the repo private until publication.

The rule for counts of distinct allele sequences (not people), which are shown exactly, is also still open.
